A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CPT policy-gradient research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite substantial reorganization and a revised title.

before.justification: V2 reports original simulations involving grids, traffic control, electricity management, Bitcoin trading, and MuJoCo, plus policy-class and batch-size experiments in Appendix I.

after.justification: V3 retains original simulation results and adds gain/loss bandit experiments in Section 5 and Appendix K.1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces the single scored trajectory with an m-trajectory mean score and replaces constant alpha with a step-size sequence. The distortion factor multiplies this mean score. The CPT objective, underlying policy-gradient formula, and quantile construction remain; newly described history inputs do not establish an architectural change.

E1.justification: V3 adds gain and loss bandit scenarios that reverse reward signs while retaining the same behavioral parameters. Existing grid, traffic, electricity, Bitcoin, and MuJoCo coverage remains. Financial trading was already evaluated in v2's appendix; its promotion to the main text is not new coverage.

E2.justification: Standard/vanilla PG, exponential risk-sensitive PG, and CPT-SPSA-G were already evaluated in v2. V3 reuses the PG comparators for its new bandits, while the retained RiskyGridworld, traffic, and scalability comparisons preserve their comparator membership.

E3.justification: The added bandits introduce a controlled evaluation using shared utility parameters across gains and losses, softmax policies, and the Adam settings in Table 2, including learning rate 0.01 and batch size 10. Retained finance and MuJoCo hyperparameters are unchanged. Additional history-input descriptions are disclosures rather than demonstrated protocol revisions.

E4.justification: V3 adds controlled illustrations of the reflection effect and a stochastic bandit policy. It removes the grid utility-sensitivity learning curves from v2 Figure 2's left panel, although grid policy examples remain. Existing batch-size, Markovian versus non-Markovian, and financial utility-sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 Figure 1 newly specifies five independent runs with different seeds and one-standard-deviation bands for the bandits. Retained experiments preserve their run counts and standard-deviation or interquartile reporting conventions; there is no evidence of increased replication of those experiments.

E6.justification: New Figure 1 reports CPT-PG choosing safely over gains and riskily over losses, while exponential risk-sensitive PG remains safe in both; Figure 12 adds a stochastic-policy result. V2's grid utility learning curves are removed. Matched scalability, traffic, electricity, finance, and MuJoCo plots retain their results.

T1.justification: V3 adds Propositions 5–7 and Appendix J, claiming estimator consistency, high-probability sample complexity with logarithmic parameter-dimension dependence, and asymptotic convergence. It removes v2's state-augmentation construction and detailed proofs of the EUT policy-characterization results, retaining their conclusions through citations. The principal policy-gradient theorem and alternative integration derivations remain.

C1.justification: V2 presents optimal-policy characterization as an original central contribution. V3 removes that contribution from its abstract and introduction and foregrounds estimator consistency, sample complexity, and convergence without increasing batch sizes. The first-order CPT-PG approach and scalability claim remain central.

C2.justification: V3 adds a reflection-effect interpretation of the bandits and discusses the adequacy and limitations of limited-history policy networks. Its broader-impact statement adds concerns about preference modeling and learned-function biases. Conversely, v2's detailed discussion of relaxing utility monotonicity is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix K adds batch-size and history-input disclosures, PyTorch usage, additional hardware, approximate runtimes, and bandit hyperparameters. The shortened electricity section loses details such as twelve two-hour slots starting at 6 a.m. and the production/pricing assumptions. These documentation changes do not establish changes to retained experiments.

R1.justification: V3 attributes EUT determinism and affine/exponential utility characterization to Bäuerle and Rieder (2014), replacing v2's presentation as original results. It also adds risk-sensitive RL and gradient-analysis references. This substantially revises novelty attribution and research positioning, beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution narrative, and conclusion are revised. Optimal-policy discussion is condensed into Section 2.3 and Appendix G.1, the method receives subsections, and convergence becomes a separate section. The healthcare example moves to an appendix, and application quotations are substantially shortened.

P2.justification: V3 adds bandit panels, merges the financial plots into main-text Figure 3, and relocates and regroups traffic and electricity displays in the appendices. It removes the grid utility panel, an EUT-proof diagram, and the experiment-summary table, while adding a bandit hyperparameter table. Typography and theorem-box presentation also change.

improvement.justification: V3 adds useful bandit controls and clearer attribution of the EUT results. However, its new theoretical centerpiece has unresolved problems: Algorithm 1 and Appendix J.2 separate the distortion factor from the averaged score, whereas Theorem 3 requires their joint expectation. Section 4 also asserts fixed-batch unbiasedness despite the finite-batch gradient bias retained in Appendix K.3, which v2 acknowledged. These concerns coexist with improved exposition and additional documentation, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
